questions.question: What are iterators and Enumerable in Ruby?
questions.title: Iterators and Enumerable
questions.direct_answer: An iterator is a method that calls a block for each element: [1,2,3].each { |x| puts x }. Enumerable is a mixin (Array, Hash, Range include it) that adds map, select, reject, find, reduce, sort, sort_by, group_by, count, include?, min/max, and more. The essentials: each (iterate, no transform), map (transform -> new array), select/filter (keep matches), reject (drop), find/detect (first match), reduce/inject (fold to one value), sort/sort_by (order), group_by (group by key -> hash), flat_map (map + flatten one level). An iterator returns: each returns the original; map/select return a new array; reduce returns one value. They chain: nums.select{|n| n.even?}.map{|n| n*10}. Enumerable needs you to define each (and optionally <=>) to get all the rest.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know iterators (each/map/select) and that Enumerable adds map/select/reduce/find/sort/group_by to collections.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using each when you want map (each returns the original; map returns a new array), or forgetting they chain.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Iterators call a block per element (each). Enumerable adds map/select/find/reduce/sort/group_by. each returns original; map returns new; reduce returns one. They chain.

sections.title: Iterators and Enumerable
sections.content:
```ruby
# Iterators call a block per element:
[1, 2, 3].each { |x| puts x }        # iterate; returns the ORIGINAL array

# Enumerable (mixed into Array/Hash/Range) adds many:
[1, 2, 3, 4].map { |n| n * 2 }      # [2, 4, 6, 8]   (new array)
[1, 2, 3, 4].select { |n| n.even? } # [2, 4]         (keep)
[1, 2, 3, 4].reject { |n| n.even? } # [1, 3]         (drop)
[1, 2, 3].find { |n| n > 2 }       # 3              (first match)
[1, 2, 3].reduce(0) { |s, n| s + n } # 6            (fold -> one value)
[3, 1, 2].sort                     # [1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2].sort_by { |n| -n }       # [3, 2, 1]      (sort by key)
%w[a b a].group_by { |c| c }       # {"a"=>["a","a"], "b"=>["b"]}
[1, 2, 3].count                    # 3
[1, 2, 3].include?(2)             # true
[1, 2, 3].min, [1, 2, 3].max       # 1, 3
[[1], [2], [3]].flat_map { |a| a } # [1, 2, 3]      (map + flatten one level)

# CHAIN (read left to right):
[1, 2, 3, 4].select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }  # [20, 40]

# To include Enumerable in your class, define `each` (and <=> for sort):
class Box
  include Enumerable
  def initialize(*xs); @xs = xs; end
  def each(&b); @xs.each(&b); end   # gives you map/select/reduce/... free
end
Box.new(1,2,3).map { |n| n * 2 }   # [2, 4, 6]
```

An iterator is a method that calls a block for each element: [1,2,3].each { |x| puts x }.

Enumerable is a mixin (Array, Hash, Range include it) that adds map, select, reject, find, reduce, sort, sort_by, group_by, count, include?, min/max, and more.

The essentials: each (iterate, no transform), map (transform -> new array), select/filter (keep matches), reject (drop), find/detect (first match), reduce/inject (fold to one value), sort/sort_by (order), group_by (group by key -> hash), flat_map (map + flatten one level). An iterator returns: each returns the original; map/select return a new array; reduce returns one value. They chain: nums.select{|n| n.even?}.map{|n| n*10}. Enumerable needs you to define each (and optionally <=>) to get all the rest.

A common mistake is using each when you want map (each returns the original; map returns a new array), or forgetting they chain.

sections.title: Iterators and Enumerable
sections.content:
```ruby
# Iterators call a block per element:
[1, 2, 3].each { |x| puts x }        # iterate; returns the ORIGINAL array

# Enumerable (mixed into Array/Hash/Range) adds many:
[1, 2, 3, 4].map { |n| n * 2 }      # [2, 4, 6, 8]   (new array)
[1, 2, 3, 4].select { |n| n.even? } # [2, 4]         (keep)
[1, 2, 3, 4].reject { |n| n.even? } # [1, 3]         (drop)
[1, 2, 3].find { |n| n > 2 }       # 3              (first match)
[1, 2, 3].reduce(0) { |s, n| s + n } # 6            (fold -> one value)
[3, 1, 2].sort                     # [1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2].sort_by { |n| -n }       # [3, 2, 1]      (sort by key)
%w[a b a].group_by { |c| c }       # {"a"=>["a","a"], "b"=>["b"]}
[1, 2, 3].count                    # 3
[1, 2, 3].include?(2)             # true
[1, 2, 3].min, [1, 2, 3].max       # 1, 3
[[1], [2], [3]].flat_map { |a| a } # [1, 2, 3]      (map + flatten one level)

# CHAIN (read left to right):
[1, 2, 3, 4].select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }  # [20, 40]

# To include Enumerable in your class, define `each` (and <=> for sort):
class Box
  include Enumerable
  def initialize(*xs); @xs = xs; end
  def each(&b); @xs.each(&b); end   # gives you map/select/reduce/... free
end
Box.new(1,2,3).map { |n| n * 2 }   # [2, 4, 6]
```
